ideas.idea: The delivery problems arise from organisational rules and system design rather than insufficient individual effort or motivation.
ideas.note: General system-design diagnosis applied to the company.

ideas.idea: The nobody-idle rule implements a Resource Topology that optimises utilisation rather than end-to-end delivery.
ideas.note: The topology explicitly aims at full resource utilisation.

ideas.idea: Assigning developers to several squads increases concurrent work and context switching, reducing focus and completion speed.
ideas.note: Direct application of the warning against multitasking.

ideas.idea: Shared developers create cross-squad waits because work stops while the needed person serves another squad.
ideas.note: Specialisation creates dependencies; blocked work accumulates.

ideas.idea: Interruptions and task switching increase cognitive sequencing errors as well as consuming attention.
ideas.note: Laboratory studies support slower switching and more errors; no company-specific magnitude.

ideas.idea: Communication overhead grows nonlinearly with team interdependencies and can reduce total productive capacity.
ideas.note: A model of communication overhead and peak team size supports the general point; exponential growth is not universal.

ideas.idea: Queueing delays grow exponentially or approach infinity as resource utilisation approaches 100%.
ideas.note: The utilisation-versus-flow problem is covered, but searches found no exponential or infinite-delay law.

ideas.idea: A system with 100% busy people necessarily has zero or near-zero flow efficiency.
ideas.note: Busy people can coexist with slow flow; the numerical zero-flow assertion is absent.

ideas.idea: Little’s Law relates cycle time to work in progress divided by throughput, so more WIP at unchanged throughput means longer cycle time.
ideas.note: The equation is explicit; it does not establish exponential growth.

ideas.idea: Increasing WIP at constant team capacity makes cycle time expand exponentially.
ideas.note: The cited relationship is linear at constant throughput; no exponential-capacity claim was found.

ideas.idea: Optimising individual components or worker utilisation in isolation can worsen the performance of the whole delivery system.
ideas.note: Both sources distinguish local busyness from overall flow.

ideas.idea: Repeatedly planning above demonstrated capacity creates predictable sprint carryover rather than extra capacity.
ideas.note: Forecasts should use past performance and actual upcoming capacity.

ideas.idea: Unfinished work accumulates across sprints and that accumulated backlog increasingly drives system behaviour.
ideas.note: Accumulations affect behaviour beyond the current inflow.

ideas.idea: Forcing firm sprint commitments beyond empirical capacity encourages burnout, poor quality, lost trust and gaming.
ideas.note: The field guide names these consequences explicitly.

ideas.idea: Time pressure, high workload and simultaneous tasks make errors and quality failures more likely.
ideas.note: These are explicit error precursors; applying them to software is permitted.

ideas.idea: A permanently overcommitted pace exhausts people and creates a reliability risk.
ideas.note: Sustainable pace and the danger of exhausted teams are explicit.

ideas.idea: The current utilisation-oriented structure conflicts with a strategy requiring fast feature delivery.
ideas.note: The primer gives this precise strategy/design mismatch.

ideas.idea: The throughput bonus encourages story-point inflation or other metric manipulation instead of real gains in customer value.
ideas.note: The source directly warns of developers moving control metrics in their own favour.

ideas.idea: Narrow quantitative throughput targets divert effort from testing, reviews, refactoring and other less visible quality work.
ideas.note: Quantity can displace less visible qualitative duties.

ideas.idea: Productivity-only bonuses and discipline for honest mistakes weaken organisational safety controls.
ideas.note: Both practices appear in the list of flawed cultural controls.

ideas.idea: Stretch targets add pressure without removing capacity constraints and can accumulate hidden operational risk.
ideas.note: Unreasonable schedule acceleration adds risk; performance still depends on constraints.

ideas.idea: Unattainable goals lose motivational force rather than reliably producing more effort.
ideas.note: The accounting text explicitly warns against unattainable ideal standards.

ideas.idea: Individual goals and bonuses can undermine teamwork when several leads depend on the same shared developers.
ideas.note: The source recommends group goals where employees depend on each other.

ideas.idea: Strong commitment to difficult goals can reduce helping and other organisational citizenship behaviours.
ideas.note: The source explicitly describes this negative relationship.

ideas.idea: Goal pressure can create easy-goal selection, unhealthy competition or sabotage.
ideas.note: These unintended consequences are explicitly enumerated.

ideas.idea: Financial incentives motivate strongly only when trust is high, performance is measurable and good performance has few negative consequences.
ideas.note: The source also requires substantial reward differences.

ideas.idea: More features or story points are outputs and do not necessarily improve customer or business outcomes.
ideas.note: The source explicitly separates output from outcomes.

ideas.idea: An output-oriented organisation can produce feature bloat and greater costs without solving customers’ problems.
ideas.note: The delivery-topology discussion warns about output without valuable outcomes.

ideas.idea: Marketing’s feature demands and engineering’s quality needs compete for the same capacity without an explicit leadership decision on the trade-off.
ideas.note: Production and prevention compete; leadership sets the conditions.

ideas.idea: Production and schedule demands tend to prevail over prevention unless leadership sustains a strong safety culture.
ideas.note: The handbook states this directly.

ideas.idea: Efficiency and thoroughness compete, so demanding more output under unchanged constraints tends to sacrifice safety or quality precautions.
ideas.note: The ETTO definition explicitly describes the trade-off.

ideas.idea: Shortcuts create technical debt whose accumulating rework costs slow later development and reduce stability.
ideas.note: Debt, interest, slower development and declining stability are explicit.

ideas.idea: Pressure to ship creates a reinforcing loop of shortcuts, defects, firefighting, reduced feature capacity and further pressure.
ideas.note: The debt cycle and fixes-that-fail mechanism directly support the loop.

ideas.idea: Bugs and instability are established as the cause of this company’s customer churn.
ideas.note: Sources connect reliability and customer value, but do not establish this company’s churn cause; E phrases part of its chain conditionally.

ideas.idea: Customers may tolerate bugs when the software delivers enough value, so bugs alone do not establish why customers leave.
ideas.note: The source explicitly discusses worthwhile benefit and the unresolved tolerance threshold.

ideas.idea: Investigate actual churn causes rather than choosing between marketing’s and engineering’s untested explanations.
ideas.note: Release economics includes customer fault costs; empiricism supports testing the explanation.

ideas.idea: Compare churned accounts with their incident and support-ticket histories to test the bug-driven churn hypothesis.
ideas.note: Reasonable empirical study design, but searches found no such churn-analysis method in the library.

ideas.idea: Quality depends on leadership’s workload and organisational decisions, so it cannot be assigned solely to engineering.
ideas.note: Leaders create the conditions for reliability and failure.

ideas.idea: Human error is a symptom of deeper weaknesses in tools, tasks and the operating system rather than a sufficient root cause.
ideas.note: The handbook explicitly states this view of human error.

ideas.idea: Stopping an investigation at the person closest to failure leaves latent weaknesses intact and creates a false belief that the problem is solved.
ideas.note: Both sources explicitly describe this investigative failure.

ideas.idea: Punishing honest errors suppresses near-miss and defect reporting, damages trust and prevents organisational learning.
ideas.note: The sources connect blame, fewer accounts and loss of reporting culture.

ideas.idea: The severity of an outage depends on failed or missing defensive controls, not simply the initiating developer error.
ideas.note: Layered controls determine severity; the company application follows directly.

ideas.idea: A just culture and psychological safety are prerequisites for trustworthy reporting and effective improvement.
ideas.note: Reporting culture and trustworthy postmortems require safety.

ideas.idea: Before individual action, use a substitution test asking whether similarly qualified peers might act the same way in the same conditions.
ideas.note: The NHS and DOE texts provide the test.

ideas.idea: The available facts conclusively establish that any comparable engineer would have made the same merge error.
ideas.note: The test is supported, but its unequivocal answer requires an investigation; other answers use qualified expectations.

ideas.idea: Use Reason’s culpability decision tree to distinguish honest system-induced errors from culpable conduct.
ideas.note: The tree and its disciplinary-policy purpose are explicit; J misidentifies the volume.

ideas.idea: Over 80% of failures or system errors are latent organisational failures and fewer than 20% are active individual errors.
ideas.note: The handbook instead gives about 80% human-error events, then about 70% of those linked to organisational weaknesses.

ideas.idea: Generic AI adoption is a symptomatic quick fix that can divert investment and attention from the underlying organisational problem.
ideas.note: The quick-fix mechanism and warning against generic AI adoption support this application.

ideas.idea: AI adoption can become a fix that initially helps but later worsens the original problem through side effects.
ideas.note: A direct application of the fixes-that-fail mechanism; no measured AI effect is implied here.

ideas.idea: Improving code-generation speed outside the actual bottleneck will not improve total throughput and can overload downstream stages.
ideas.note: TOC explicitly says non-bottleneck improvements can have no effect or add pressure downstream.

ideas.idea: Faster AI code generation into the current overloaded pipeline would increase unfinished work and review or testing queues.
ideas.note: Conditional application of upstream acceleration and new monitoring work.

ideas.idea: AI-generated code in this environment will increase production defect rates and portal outages.
ideas.note: Overload and AI errors are covered, but no source establishes the asserted defect/outage effect.

ideas.idea: Introducing AI will double the volume of unverified code entering the pipeline.
ideas.note: Downstream overload is supported; the doubling figure is absent.

ideas.idea: AI-generated work will increase false-positive defect rates.
ideas.note: Searches found no causal connection between AI code generation and false-positive defect rates.

ideas.idea: Review, testing, integration and fragmented attention are the delivery constraints rather than raw coding speed.
ideas.note: These are plausible constraints, but the sources require measuring or mapping the actual bottleneck.

ideas.idea: AI agents introduce monitoring responsibilities and processes that consume human capacity.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly predicts human monitoring work.

ideas.idea: Evaluate AI’s net value after subtracting tool access, adaptation and error-detection and correction costs from the manual-process cost.
ideas.note: The cost equation and its three components are explicit.

ideas.idea: Generic vendor claims that AI coding assistants immediately improve output by 30–40% should be weighed against system constraints.
ideas.note: Constraint and hype cautions are supported; no such vendor productivity figure was found.

ideas.idea: End multi-squad assignments and give each developer one dedicated squad.
ideas.note: A direct application of focus, reduced multitasking and cohesive team design.

ideas.idea: Limit work in progress and finish existing work before accepting new work.
ideas.note: Explicit WIP limits and focus on finishing are supported.

ideas.idea: Use smaller, simpler stories and batches rather than large epics and large volumes of simultaneous work.
ideas.note: The source recommends reducing story complexity and quantity.

ideas.idea: Set sprint forecasts from demonstrated delivery capacity, approximately 25 points here, rather than the aspirational 40.
ideas.note: Company numbers apply the historical-capacity principle.

ideas.idea: Use the last three sprints’ completed work as the planning baseline.
ideas.note: The guide recommends ideally three to four sprints of stable velocity data.

ideas.idea: Treat sprint backlogs and velocity as empirical forecasts and focusing tools, not guaranteed performance contracts.
ideas.note: The forecasting role and warning against firm commitments are explicit.

ideas.idea: Build stable cross-functional squads aligned to product capabilities so teams can deliver end-to-end with fewer dependencies.
ideas.note: Complete cross-functional delivery units are explicit.

ideas.idea: Change staffing and WIP first because fragmented attention is the common bottleneck through which the other fixes must pass.
ideas.note: Focus and constraint-first improvement are supported, but declaring this the unique first bottleneck and all other fixes ineffective is stronger than the evidence.

ideas.idea: Leadership should change the no-idle rule first because organisational design is under its control and lower-level teams cannot change the policy.
ideas.note: Internal design and leadership responsibility support the reason for priority.

ideas.idea: Start with single-squad allocation because it is cheap, reversible and can yield an interpretable experiment quickly.
ideas.note: The change is an internal policy intervention; zero cost and rapid reversibility are not established.

ideas.idea: Single-squad allocation should be judged within two or three sprints using carryover, escaped bugs and incidents.
ideas.note: Tracking work and empirical feedback are supported; the evaluation window and complete metric set are added.

ideas.idea: Judge the staffing change after one quarter by completed work and escaped defects.
ideas.note: Completed-work metrics are covered; the quarter and defect-based evaluation prescription are added.

ideas.idea: Reported points will initially fall because planning becomes more honest.
ideas.note: Plausible consequence of removing gaming, but no source predicts a necessary initial fall.

ideas.idea: Single-squad focus will immediately recover 20–30% of engineering capacity.
ideas.note: Switching costs are supported; the recovery percentage and immediacy are absent.

ideas.idea: Developers currently lose 20–40% of each day to context switching.
ideas.note: Task-switching costs are covered, but the daily percentage is absent.

ideas.idea: Cap active work at one or two items per engineer.
ideas.note: The source asks teams to choose their WIP maximum; it does not prescribe this range.

ideas.idea: Cap active epics at three across the engineering group.
ideas.note: WIP limits are supported, but no source supplies this group-wide threshold.

ideas.idea: Preserve spare capacity to absorb reviews, testing, incidents and other variability instead of maximising everyone’s busyness.
ideas.note: The source explicitly retains free resources to handle exceptions constructively.

ideas.idea: Maintain 15–20% operational slack for fast flow.
ideas.note: Slack is supported; the percentage is not.

ideas.idea: Remove or suspend the 40% throughput target and its link to squad-lead bonuses.
ideas.note: Direct response to productivity-only rewards and control-metric gaming.

ideas.idea: Pause or rescind the release developer’s performance plan while investigating the wider system.
ideas.note: Individual action needs a fair investigation of wider causes; unconditional permanent immunity is not inferred.

ideas.idea: Reopen the portal outage as a blameless systemic learning review rather than a search for a culprit.
ideas.note: The sources prescribe context-sensitive, nonjudgemental incident learning.

ideas.idea: Ask how the organisation failed the developer and what could have prevented the incident.
ideas.note: Both questions are explicit in the handbook.

ideas.idea: Repair the review, automated test, deployment and rollback defences exposed by the outage review.
ideas.note: The sources recommend verifying controls and following through on technical remediation.

ideas.idea: Make automated quality checks and code-review approval mandatory gates that stop unsafe changes from progressing.
ideas.note: Quality gates decide whether a product can proceed; security criteria can automate decisions.

ideas.idea: Prioritise restoring just culture before other operational changes because fear hides the information needed to improve.
ideas.note: Reporting and trustworthy incident analysis explicitly depend on psychological safety.

ideas.idea: Withdraw target-linked pay and pause individual punishment together before reorganising so the baseline and feedback can be trusted.
ideas.note: Removing incentives to distort and suppress information directly supports this ordering rationale.

ideas.idea: Involve engineers in owning and redesigning the change rather than merely imposing it on them.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly says people must own their change.

ideas.idea: Announce staffing changes alongside bonus removal and a renewed incident review because isolated changes will not hold.
ideas.note: Systemically reinforcing policies, rather than isolated optimisation, support the combined intervention.

ideas.idea: Replace utilisation or point-velocity targets with work-item flow measures such as lead time, cycle time and completed-work throughput.
ideas.note: Work-item rather than people metrics and the named flow metrics are explicit.

ideas.idea: Track escaped defects alongside completed work so improved output cannot conceal worsening quality.
ideas.note: Combining qualitative performance with output measurement follows directly; the particular defect measure is a company application.

ideas.idea: Track restoration time or change-failure rates to assess reliability rather than rewarding raw velocity.
ideas.note: Incident timings and reliability improvement are covered, but the prescribed MTTR/change-failure metric regime is not.

ideas.idea: Use Unbroken Customer Flow Time as a replacement engineering performance metric.
ideas.note: No occurrence or definition of this named metric was found.

ideas.idea: Give product, marketing and engineering shared customer or business outcome goals instead of independent feature-volume targets.
ideas.note: Shared interdependent goals and outcome orientation support the recommendation.

ideas.idea: Evaluate or reward leads on customer retention, satisfaction, reliability and aggregate business outcomes rather than story points.
ideas.note: Group/outcome goals and goal-contingent reward principles support this application.

ideas.idea: Review completed work, carryover, customer defects and restoration time together without paying against those measures.
ideas.note: The non-incentivised diagnostic use is supported; the exact four-measure package, including restoration time, is added.

ideas.idea: Put one respected Product Owner in charge of each product line’s backlog so stakeholder demands are reconciled in one place.
ideas.note: The Product Owner is one person representing stakeholders and the organisation must respect the decisions.

ideas.idea: Separate authority to hold an unsafe release from management of the growth schedule and budget.
ideas.note: Independent technical authority separate from schedule and funding is explicit.

ideas.idea: Use cost of delay divided by job size to prioritise smaller high-value work collaboratively across product, marketing and engineering.
ideas.note: WSJF and its formula are explicit; collaborative use is a direct application.

ideas.idea: Create an explicit governance agreement that reserves capacity for growth features, debt remediation and reliability work.
ideas.note: Explicitly balancing project constraints and managing debt in the backlog support the general agreement.

ideas.idea: Allocate sprint capacity as 70% growth features, 20% architecture and debt, and 10% infrastructure and reliability.
ideas.note: The priority matrix balances time, cost and scope; it supplies no 70/20/10 allocation.

ideas.idea: Offer marketing a predictable cadence of finished features instead of promising one feature every week.
ideas.note: Predictable delivery and empirical capacity support the revised promise.

ideas.idea: Include the release-safety work discovered by the outage review in the squad’s planned workload.
ideas.note: Remediation must be acted on and forecasts must account for real capacity.

ideas.idea: Defer broad AI rollout until flow and release defences have stabilised.
ideas.note: Constraint-first investment supports deferring non-bottleneck automation.

ideas.idea: Aim AI at a specifically identified bottleneck instead of adopting it generically.
ideas.note: The primer states this advice explicitly.

ideas.idea: Direct AI investment specifically towards test generation, review verification, static analysis and deployment checks.
ideas.note: Targeted AI and automated checks are supported separately; AI effectiveness for this prescribed set is not established.

ideas.idea: Pilot AI on one constraint, budget for human review and compare the results before and after.
ideas.note: Targeting, monitoring and empirical inspection support this application.

ideas.idea: Use AI to broaden teams’ skills and work mandates so they can eliminate external dependencies and deliver more end-to-end.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly associates AI with broader mandates and organisational elevation.

ideas.idea: AI can make scarce expertise more available and enable broader organisational capabilities.
ideas.note: The primer advances this proposition; support here records a source statement, not empirical verification.

ideas.idea: AI’s promise of expanding expertise conflicts with warnings that technical quick fixes and non-bottleneck capacity can worsen the system.
ideas.note: Both positions are present; they can be reconciled by targeting the actual constraint.

ideas.idea: Difficult, specific and accepted goals can raise effort and performance, creating a tension with warnings about gaming and quality loss.
ideas.note: Goal-setting benefits are conditional, while control-metric gaming is a separate risk.

ideas.idea: Deming’s process-improvement approach warns that numerical goals narrow attention and create fear, in contrast to stretch-goal motivation.
ideas.note: The source explicitly contrasts TQM process orientation and goal setting.

ideas.idea: Stretch goals are appropriate for simple independent tasks but cause gaming in complex software engineering.
ideas.note: Narrowing and gaming risks are supported; this categorical task-complexity boundary is not.

ideas.idea: Money tied to goals may strengthen commitment while extrinsic rewards can also crowd out intrinsic motivation.
ideas.note: Both motivational mechanisms are stated.

ideas.idea: Effective hard goals require acceptance, commitment, sufficient ability and the absence of blocking constraints.
ideas.note: The complete set of conditions is explicit.

ideas.idea: Let squads participate in setting achievable customer-outcome goals to increase ownership and commitment.
ideas.note: Participation and bottom-up, outcome-focused goal setting are explicit.

ideas.idea: The OKR case for stretch goals assumes collaborative, outcome-focused goal setting, which differs from imposed point targets tied to pay.
ideas.note: The underlying goal-setting conditions differ; the passages support that distinction.

ideas.idea: A goal-setting framework can produce a threefold productivity increase within twelve months.
ideas.note: The source repeats an Align vendor claim; the answer identifies that provenance.

ideas.idea: Utilisation-oriented resource management conflicts with flow-oriented approaches that preserve focus and spare capacity.
ideas.note: The contrast exists in the library; it need not be attributed to all classical management.

ideas.idea: Classical accounting and Taylorist management require 100% labour utilisation and regard idle developer time as wasted payroll.
ideas.note: The Resource Topology supports a utilisation aim, but the universal accounting/Taylorist doctrine and payroll assertions were not found.

ideas.idea: Resource Topology is suitable for some temporary specialist engagements, so utilisation is not inherently wrong in every setting.
ideas.note: The primer explicitly justifies the topology for temporary relationships.

ideas.idea: Pure blameless models hold that all human error is entirely system-induced and discipline is always counterproductive.
ideas.note: Learning reviews protect participants, but the guide retains discipline elsewhere and excludes intentional harm; the absolute characterisation is not supported.

ideas.idea: Just culture preserves individual responsibility and possible management action for culpable conduct while rejecting automatic punishment for honest errors.
ideas.note: NHS/DOE retain a fair route to individual action; CAIB also retains responsibility.

ideas.idea: Keep disciplinary or personal-accountability processes separate from the safety learning review.
ideas.note: The learning-review firewall is explicit.

ideas.idea: NHS and DOE preserve a route to individual action, CAIB separates personal accountability, and the Forest Service forbids using learning-review findings for discipline.
ideas.note: These are different process boundaries, not a disagreement over whether any accountability exists.

ideas.idea: The Forest Service defines accountability as giving an honest account and obliges the organisation to learn and improve its conditions.
ideas.note: Forward-looking accountability is explicitly defined.

ideas.idea: Traditional individual performance-reward models pull against safety approaches that locate the conditions for failure in organisational design.
ideas.note: Individual contingent rewards coexist with systemic explanations; the sources do not mandate scapegoating.

ideas.idea: Traditional HR doctrine specifically advocates PIPs and punishment after honest operational errors as a deterrent to carelessness.
ideas.note: Performance management and rewards exist, but this specific pro-punishment doctrine is not supported.

ideas.idea: DOE root-cause prevention conflicts with the Forest Service’s emphasis on networked conditions and avoiding causal statements.
ideas.note: The differing investigative approaches are explicit.

ideas.idea: Formal postmortem recommendations can add complexity, increase risk and obstruct learning.
ideas.note: The guide explicitly warns about this effect.

ideas.idea: Write a shared incident account first, then a short list of corrective actions with named owners.
ideas.note: The Learning Review builds on an FLA account and creates an action plan with responsibilities.

ideas.idea: Org Topologies calls for changes to surrounding structures whereas Kanban permits starting with existing titles and roles.
ideas.note: Incremental starting points and wider organisational design can coexist.

ideas.idea: If single-squad allocation cannot hold, reconsider the wider arrangement of nine squads across the product lines.
ideas.note: A direct application of changing reinforcing structures when a local change is insufficient.

ideas.idea: Scrum’s fixed timeboxed iterations contrast with Kanban’s continuous pull flow and explicit WIP controls.
ideas.note: The scheduling approaches differ, though the sources do not make them mutually exclusive.

ideas.idea: Scrum requires fixed sprint deliverable commitments and Kanban holds that such commitments create sprint-end rushing and truncated testing.
ideas.note: Scrum commits to a goal with flexible scope; the field guide rejects firm backlog guarantees, and no sprint-end claim was found.

ideas.idea: Technical and organisational changes can initially increase error risk and create new failure modes through added complexity.
ideas.note: Both sources warn about complex changes and unintended consequences.

ideas.idea: Treat system archetypes as hypotheses and test the diagnosis with squads rather than imposing a convenient label.
ideas.note: The brief warns against jumping to archetypes and external labels.

ideas.idea: Frontline employees know operational problems that executives cannot see, making safe upward feedback essential.
ideas.note: The source reports Yoshida’s 4% executive versus 100% employee awareness figures.

ideas.idea: Code-review outcomes are sensitive to patch size and review burden, so larger incoming changes create review risk.
ideas.note: The WebKit/Mozilla review study discusses patch size and review time.

ideas.idea: Aggressive schedules can be healthy, but their effects on safety must be monitored rather than automatically taking precedence.
ideas.note: The board explicitly makes both points.

ideas.idea: People under schedule pressure can become reluctant to say that a date cannot or should not be met.
ideas.note: CAIB describes the difficulty of admitting excessive schedule and resource strain.

ideas.idea: Leadership must align goals, resources and safety and take responsibility for the conditions its policies create.
ideas.note: The board directly assigns this responsibility to leaders.

ideas.idea: Software-productivity folklore, such as the 28-to-1 developer claim, is a poor basis for accepting unmeasured AI productivity promises.
ideas.note: Jones explains the evidential vacuum and the misinterpreted productivity claim; applying the caution to new promises is direct.

ideas.idea: Technical quality as customer value conflicts with an economic view that customers accept faults when benefits outweigh them.
ideas.note: Open Kanban defines software value as good-quality working code; Jones describes tolerated faults.

ideas.idea: Use service quality and customer value across product and engineering to sustain satisfaction, loyalty and profitable growth.
ideas.note: The service-profit chain connects value, satisfaction, loyalty and profitability.
